title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 49–50
description: Curated B2 fixed expressions for emotions, moods, physical feelings, problem situations, consequences and responses.

units.title: Unit 49 — Emotions and moods
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 49. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Understand fixed, mainly informal expressions for happiness, sadness, mood, health and fear.
Distinguish literal states from figurative phrases such as under the weather, at death’s door and on cloud nine.
Use idioms describing composure, intense emotions, excitement and improvement in natural contexts.
Recognise the often exaggerated, light-hearted tone and limits of formality of these expressions.

sectionsChecked: A: Positive feelings, moods and states
B: Negative feelings, moods and states
E: Other expressions for actions and feelings
Language help: figurative exaggeration and informal register

items.section: A · Positive feelings, moods and states
items.example: She was on cloud nine after receiving the scholarship.
items.note: Informal idiom for being extremely pleased or happy.

items.section: A · Positive feelings, moods and states
items.example: Despite the early start, everyone was in high spirits.
items.note: Describes a lively, cheerful mood in a person or group.

items.section: A · Positive feelings, moods and states
items.example: Keep your chin up; one difficult interview does not decide your future.
items.note: Encourages someone to stay cheerful despite disappointment or trouble.

items.section: A · Positive feelings, moods and states
items.example: Since moving closer to her family, she has been as happy as Larry.
items.note: Informal British comparison meaning extremely happy; Larry is part of the fixed phrase.

items.section: A · Positive feelings, moods and states
items.example: The children were as happy as can be on their first camping trip.
items.note: Another emphatic way of saying very happy.

items.pt: estar com cara triste; fazer cara de desânimo
items.section: B · Negative feelings, moods and states
items.example: Why have you got such a long face today?
items.note: Used about someone whose face shows sadness or disappointment.

items.section: B · Negative feelings, moods and states
items.example: After the project was cancelled, the whole team felt down in the dumps.
items.note: Informal expression for being sad or low in spirits.

items.section: B · Negative feelings, moods and states
items.example: I was in a bad mood after sleeping badly.
items.note: Mood is a temporary emotional state; use in a bad mood.

items.word: like a bear with a sore head
items.section: B · Negative feelings, moods and states
items.example: The manager was like a bear with a sore head all morning.
items.note: Informal British simile for being extremely irritable.

items.pt: dar um chilique; ter um ataque de raiva
items.section: B · Negative feelings, moods and states
items.example: He threw a wobbly when he realised the flight had been cancelled.
items.note: Informal British phrase for suddenly becoming very angry or upset; past: threw a wobbly.

items.section: C · Physical feelings and states
items.example: I was completely done in after the long hike.
items.note: Informal expression meaning physically or mentally exhausted.

items.section: C · Physical feelings and states
items.example: I am feeling a little under the weather, so I will rest today.
items.note: Informal phrase for feeling slightly unwell, not usually dangerously ill.

items.pt: em excelente forma; no seu melhor desempenho
items.section: C · Physical feelings and states
items.example: The goalkeeper was on top form throughout the match.
items.note: Means performing or feeling exceptionally well; often about sport or health.

items.pt: estar tonto; estar com a cabeça girando
items.section: C · Physical feelings and states
items.example: My head was spinning after I stood up too quickly.
items.note: Describes dizziness; the possessive changes with the subject.

items.pt: às portas da morte; muito mal de saúde
items.section: C · Physical feelings and states
items.example: He claimed he was at death’s door, though he only had a mild cold.
items.note: An exaggerated, often humorous expression for being extremely ill.

items.pt: com uma saúde de ferro; em ótima forma
items.section: C · Physical feelings and states
items.example: My grandmother walks every morning and is as fit as a fiddle.
items.note: Means very healthy and physically fit.

items.section: D · Fear and fright
items.example: I was scared stiff during the thunderstorm.
items.note: Strong informal expression for being extremely frightened.

items.word: frighten the life out of someone
items.pt: dar um susto enorme em alguém; apavorar alguém
items.section: D · Fear and fright
items.example: That unexpected knock frightened the life out of me.
items.note: Pattern: frighten the life out of someone. Often describes a sudden, intense fright.
items.speechText: frighten the life out of me

items.section: D · Fear and fright
items.example: The thought of speaking to a thousand people made him shake in his boots.
items.note: Idiomatic fear expression; shake in your shoes is also possible.

items.section: D · Fear and fright
items.example: We were scared out of our wits when the alarm sounded.
items.note: Informal, emphatic expression for very strong fear.

items.pt: levar um baita susto; quase pular de susto
items.section: D · Fear and fright
items.example: I nearly jumped out of my skin when the dog barked behind me.
items.note: A sudden, involuntary reaction to an unexpected noise or surprise.

items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: We got carried away with our plans and forgot to check the cost.
items.note: Become too enthusiastic or excited and lose perspective; get carried away by or with something.

items.pt: manter a cabeça fria; manter a calma
items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: Try to keep a cool head when the meeting becomes tense.
items.note: Stay calm and think clearly in a difficult situation.

items.pt: levar as coisas como elas vêm; lidar com cada situação quando surgir
items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: She prefers to take everything as it comes rather than worry about the future.
items.note: Respond calmly to events as they happen instead of planning or worrying excessively.

items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: After several difficult months, things are finally looking up.
items.note: Means circumstances are improving; looking up is not literal here.

items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: He swelled with pride as his daughter accepted her award.
items.note: Become very proud, often of one’s own or another person’s achievement.

items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: She felt on top of the world after passing her final examination.
items.note: Informal expression for feeling extremely happy or successful.

items.word: as happy as the day is long
items.section: E · Responses, feelings and changing fortunes
items.example: The new parents seemed as happy as the day is long.
items.note: Another emphatic fixed comparison for being very happy; used in exercise 49.1.

units.title: Unit 50 — Commenting on problematic situations
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 50. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish types of difficulty, including chaos, disaster, dilemma, challenges and being in a fix.
Use vocabulary for the causes and effects of disruption, deprivation, irritation and lack with accurate prepositions.
Contrast idioms for actively confronting problems, calming tensions, avoiding responsibilities and exposing causes.
Describe turning points, dead ends, reconciliation and the concealment or resolution of difficulties.

sectionsChecked: A: Types of problems and difficulties
B: Specific difficulties and related noun forms
C: Idioms for dealing with difficulties
D: Idioms for changes in problem situations

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: There was complete chaos at the station after the power failure.
items.note: A state of confusion without order; common phrases include in chaos and utter chaos.

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: The unexpected flood was a disaster for nearby farms.
items.note: An event causing great harm or damage; can also describe a serious failure.

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: The committee faced a dilemma about how to allocate the limited budget.
items.note: A situation requiring a difficult choice between alternatives; face a dilemma or be in a dilemma.

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: We face a dilemma: postpone the launch or accept additional risk.
items.note: Natural collocation: face a dilemma about whether to do something.

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: I am in a fix because I have lost my keys and my phone battery is flat.
items.note: Informal way of saying you are in a difficult situation.

items.pt: num beco sem saída; numa situação difícil de resolver
items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: The sudden deadline put the research team in a tight corner.
items.note: A difficult situation with few ways out; often get into a tight corner.

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: I got into a muddle when I tried to follow the complicated instructions.
items.note: British English: confused or mixed up, particularly about information or organisation.

items.section: A · Types of problems and difficulties
items.example: Designing a reliable control system is a demanding challenge.
items.note: A more positive framing of a problem, emphasising the effort and ability it requires.

items.pt: muito prejudicado por; bastante afetado por
items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: Small businesses were badly affected by the extended power cut.
items.note: Passive pattern: be affected by something; badly signals a serious negative impact.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The background hum is mildly irritating but does not stop me working.
items.note: Mildly weakens the degree of irritation.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The repeated error messages became intensely annoying.
items.note: Intensely increases the strength of the negative feeling.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: Unexpected maintenance work disrupted the morning experiments.
items.note: To prevent normal progress or a plan from continuing as intended.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The rail strike caused major disruption across the region.
items.note: Noun form of disrupt; often cause disruption to a service.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The negotiations collapsed after the parties failed to agree.
items.note: A building can physically collapse; talks or plans can collapse figuratively.

items.pt: ser privado de; ficar sem algo necessário ou valioso
items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: Children should not be deprived of regular opportunities to play.
items.note: Passive construction: be deprived of something, not deprived from.

items.pt: privação; falta prolongada de algo essencial
items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: Long-term sleep deprivation can affect concentration.
items.note: Noun corresponding to deprive; common collocation: sleep deprivation.

items.pt: partir o coração de alguém; causar muita tristeza
items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: It broke her heart to leave the place where she grew up.
items.note: Strong emotional effect; the past form is broke someone’s heart.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The family experienced heartbreak after the sudden loss.
items.note: Noun for extreme sadness; related to break someone’s heart.

items.pt: faltar; não ter o suficiente de; falta
items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The proposal lacks convincing evidence.
items.note: Verb: lack something (no of). Noun: a lack of something.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: A lack of planning caused delays in the project.
items.note: Noun phrase: a lack of something; contrast with the verb lack something.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The noise had a noticeable effect on everyone’s concentration.
items.note: Often have an effect on; distinguish noun effect from verb affect.

items.pt: ter um efeito profundo sobre; impactar profundamente
items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: Meeting her former teacher had a profound effect on her career plans.
items.note: Strong collocation from the exercise: profound effect on someone or something.
items.speechText: have a profound effect on health

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: The constant notifications became a major irritant.
items.note: Noun for something that causes irritation.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: To her irritation, the same mistake happened again.
items.note: Noun related to irritating; also used for physical irritation.

items.section: B · Specific difficulties and their effects
items.example: He tried to hide his annoyance when the meeting ran late.
items.note: Noun related to annoying; often express or show annoyance.

items.pt: ficar em segundo plano; deixar os outros assumirem
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: During the negotiations, I decided to take a back seat and let the experts speak.
items.note: Step aside and allow others to act or lead; contrasts with take the bull by the horns.

items.word: take the bull by the horns
items.pt: enfrentar o problema de frente; pegar o touro pelos chifres
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: We finally took the bull by the horns and redesigned the faulty system.
items.note: Act decisively to confront a difficult situation rather than avoiding it.

items.pt: agitar os ânimos; piorar a situação
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: Repeating that rumour will only stir things up.
items.note: Make a difficult or tense situation worse, often by provoking conflict.

items.pt: apaziguar os ânimos; acalmar os conflitos
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: The chair tried to pour oil on troubled waters after the heated debate.
items.note: Say or do something to calm a tense situation; contrasts with stir things up.

items.pt: não suportar a ideia de; não ter coragem ou disposição para enfrentar
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: I can’t face sorting through all those old boxes tonight.
items.note: Pattern: can’t face + noun or -ing, or can’t face the thought of + -ing.

items.word: lay your cards on the table
items.pt: abrir o jogo; deixar sua posição bem clara
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: Before we sign the agreement, I want to lay my cards on the table.
items.note: State your position or intentions openly and frankly.

items.pt: organizar-se; tomar jeito; pôr as coisas em ordem
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: We need to get our act together before the inspection next week.
items.note: Informal: become organised and begin acting effectively.

items.word: get to the bottom of things
items.pt: descobrir a verdade; esclarecer o que realmente aconteceu
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: The team examined the logs to get to the bottom of things.
items.note: Investigate until the real cause or explanation is understood.

items.pt: prestar atenção de verdade; passar a dar importância
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: The surprising results made the committee sit up and take notice.
items.note: Start paying serious attention, especially after an important development.

items.pt: começar a entender; adquirir compreensão de
items.section: C · Dealing with problems
items.example: It took me several days to get a grasp of the new protocol.
items.note: Understand the essentials of something complex; also have a grasp of.
items.speechText: get a grasp of the situation

items.pt: a situação virou; as coisas mudaram para melhor
items.section: D · Changes and outcomes in difficult situations
items.example: After months of poor results, the tide has finally turned for the team.
items.note: The course of events has changed; often implies improvement after setbacks.

items.word: see the light at the end of the tunnel
items.pt: ver uma luz no fim do túnel
items.section: D · Changes and outcomes in difficult situations
items.example: After several rounds of testing, we can finally see the light at the end of the tunnel.
items.note: See signs that a long and difficult period may soon be over.

items.pt: chegar a um beco sem saída; ficar sem perspectivas de avanço
items.section: D · Changes and outcomes in difficult situations
items.example: Our investigation came to a dead end when the records disappeared.
items.note: Reach a stage where no further progress is possible.

items.pt: chegar a um ponto de virada
items.section: D · Changes and outcomes in difficult situations
items.example: Finishing the first prototype marked a turning point in the project.
items.note: Reach a moment when a situation or direction starts to change.

items.pt: fazer as pazes; deixar as diferenças de lado
items.section: D · Changes and outcomes in difficult situations
items.example: After years of disagreement, the neighbours agreed to bury the hatchet.
items.note: Stop quarrelling and make peace; informal idiom.

items.pt: varrer um problema para debaixo do tapete; encobrir
items.section: D · Changes and outcomes in difficult situations
items.example: The company should investigate the complaint instead of sweeping it under the carpet.
items.note: Deliberately hide or ignore a problem rather than solving it.
